# Your Phone Does Not Need to Ring to Break Your Focus

Imagine you are reading, studying, or working.

Your phone is on the desk. You do not touch it. You do not even look at the screen.

Then comes a short notification sound.

You keep your eyes on your work. But your attention may already have moved.

A study published in 2022 tested this idea with 73 university students. They completed a simple visual task many times. Some rounds included a phone notification sound. Other rounds included a neutral sound.

The students did not look at or touch a phone during the task.

Even so, they answered more slowly after hearing the notification sound. A brain-wave signal was also larger. The researchers understood this as a sign that the students needed extra mental effort to keep working.

In other words, the sound seemed to catch their attention automatically. They did not make a clear decision to stop working. Their minds reacted first.

But the story does not end with sound.

A second study, published in 2023, looked at a silent phone. Forty-two university students took a concentration test. Their phones were turned off, and no notification arrived.

When the phone was on the desk, the average attention score was about 100. When the phone was moved to another room, it rose to about 109.

Their speed score showed a similar difference: about 98 with the phone on the desk, compared with about 109 when the phone was away.

The researchers found this lower performance even without a sound or a screen. They suggested that the phone’s presence may leave part of the mind ready for a possible message.

### The habit begins before the first message

This may help explain why checking a phone can feel difficult to stop. In a 2018 survey, 72% of US teenagers said they often or sometimes checked messages or notifications soon after waking up. About four in ten said they felt worried, upset, or lonely when their phone was not nearby. A majority also felt they should reply quickly to messages.

These answers describe teenagers’ experiences. They do not prove that phones caused those feelings. But they show how closely phone checking can be tied to daily life.

### A pattern, not a rule for everyone

The experiments involved university students, while the survey asked US teenagers. So these findings show a pattern in particular groups and conditions. They do not mean that every person loses focus every time a phone makes a sound. They also do not diagnose a medical addiction.

## In one line…

A notification can take a piece of your attention without being opened, and a silent phone may still matter before it rings. “I did not check it” does not necessarily mean “it had no effect.”

# Why a Notification Can Steal Focus Before You Check Your Phone

Imagine you are working. Your phone makes a sound. You do not pick it up or even look at the screen. Still, the moment feels different. Research suggests that distraction may begin before you check.

Two peer-reviewed studies help explain why. In a 2022 study, 73 university students completed a visual task while either a notification sound or an unrelated comparison sound played. They did not look at or touch a phone. Even so, the sound affected how they handled the task.

A 2023 study examined a quieter situation. Forty-two university students took a concentration test with a powered-off smartphone on the desk or in another room. No notifications were received. This study also found a difference between the two settings.

At first, this seems like a story about willpower. But the studies point to two separate pressures. One comes from the sound. The other comes from the device being part of the workspace. Together, they suggest that “not checking” is not the same as “not being affected.” The studies used specific tasks and university students, so they do not show that every phone affects every person in every situation.

Outside the lab, this pull is also part of daily life for many US teens. In a 2018 survey of teens aged 13 to 17, 72% said they often or sometimes checked messages or notifications soon after waking. When their phone was not with them, 56% reported feeling anxious, lonely, upset, or some combination of these. A majority also said they felt a need to reply quickly to texts, social-media messages, or other notifications.

### The hidden cost comes before the check

The key shift is from behavior to effort. A person can keep their hands off the phone and still pay a price on the very trial when the sound appears. Responses were slower, while a brain-wave signal associated with cognitive control became larger. The researchers interpreted this as a sign that staying on task required extra mental effort after the notification sound.

### A quiet phone can still take up space

The second experiment did not compare a ringing phone with a silent phone. It compared a powered-off phone on the desk with that phone in another room. Attention scores were about 100 versus 109, and processing-speed scores were about 98 versus 109. For work or study, moving the device may address something that muting does not.

## In one line...

A notification may interrupt focus through its sound, while a silent phone may still compete through its presence. Protecting attention may involve not only resisting the urge to check, but also reducing the phone’s chance to enter the task.

# The Café Question: Guest, Worker, or Both?

A café is no longer only a place for coffee and conversation. For some people, it is also a place to work for hours with a laptop. These “customer-workers” buy something, take a seat, and use a public space for work-related tasks.

For café owners, this creates a difficult choice. Should they welcome this customer group, or protect the space for shorter visits and social use? Two recent sources show that both answers are now being tested.

A 2021 qualitative study by L. Mimoun and A. Gruen, published in the *Journal of Service Research*, examined this question. In London, it covered 38 third places. Researchers made 52 observation visits, interviewed 27 customers and 12 service providers, and reviewed 55 media sources.

The study places these businesses into four groups. Archetypal places discourage work. Status Quo places do not clearly choose between workers and social customers, and this is where conflict is described as strongest. Compromise places try to serve both groups but may struggle to enforce their rules. Productive Third Places, or PTPs, clearly target customer-workers and adapt the space for them.

The other response is restriction. In a report published by *Coffee Intelligence* on April 28, 2026, The Barn introduced a one-hour laptop limit, or a full laptop ban on certain busy days. At its Neukölln store in Berlin, the café reported that laptop users occupied more than 70 percent of seats for long periods. It also reported a 25 percent loss in sales before the policy change.

The Barn’s founder, Ralf Rüller, said the business wants to offer an excellent coffee experience. At the same time, he recognizes the demand from remote workers who want to work in cafés.

So the debate is not simply about laptops. It is about whether a café treats work as a problem, a compromise, or a planned part of its identity.

### Design can welcome—or quietly resist—work

Design can make a policy clear without a sign. Some places offer no Wi-Fi, play loud music, or use less comfortable chairs to discourage work. PTPs choose the opposite: dependable Wi-Fi, enough power outlets, useful furniture, controlled noise, and daily offers.

### The real product is the atmosphere

The study suggests that PTPs may gain more than a payment from customer-workers. They may bring steadier income in quiet hours, use seats that might otherwise be empty, and make the café look lively. But these are interpreted benefits, not guaranteed results.

## In one line…

Cafés are not simply deciding whether laptops belong. They are deciding what kind of place they want to be—and how clearly they will design and manage it.

# 📦 The Strange Pull of the Refresh Button

Why do we open a delivery page again and again?

The answer may begin with the waiting, not the package.

When the result is unknown, checking for new information can feel like taking a small action in a situation we cannot control.

In 2025, Howell and Sweeny reported a long-term study in *Emotion*. They followed three groups for several weeks or months: people waiting for the result of the 2020 U.S. presidential election, people waiting for California bar exam results, and people waiting for academic job decisions.

They found a clear pattern. As people’s worry grew, they checked the news and searched for updates more often.

This does not prove that worry directly caused the checking. But it shows that worry and information-seeking moved together. The finding is surprising because people often think anxiety makes us avoid information. In these waiting periods, people searched more when their worry was at its highest.

Checking may create a weak and temporary feeling of control. It does not change the final result. Still, it gives the person something to do. When that feeling disappears, another check may seem necessary.

The studies did not test delivery tracking pages directly. But they offer a possible explanation for why a simple refresh button can become so hard to ignore.

### Uncertainty makes checking more tempting

A 2021 study in *Scientific Reports* looked at this question in a lab. Twenty-eight healthy people, aged 19 to 29, watched moving dots and judged their direction. Before answering, they could replay the dots as many times as they wanted.

When the movement was harder to understand, they checked more often. The reported result was strong: *b* was 0.90, with *p* below 2 × 10⁻¹⁶. This supports a link between uncertainty and checking, but it does not prove the same direct effect on delivery tracking.

### Noticing doubt may keep the loop going

The same study found that people who could consciously notice their own uncertainty were more likely to change their checking as the task became harder. A measure of uncertainty outside conscious awareness did not predict the pattern.

In simple terms, the thought “I am not sure” may bring the hand back to the button. The study was small, so this is a clue about the pattern, not a diagnosis of any person.

## In one line…

When the outcome is out of our hands, refreshing can feel like taking control. But that brief feeling may also keep the waiting—and the checking—alive.

# Assigned Desks Are Quietly Coming Back to Some Offices

One office question is quietly coming back:

**“Where is my desk?”**

After the pandemic, many companies adopted **hot-desking**. Workers were not given one permanent desk. Instead, they chose an open desk when they arrived.

The system allowed companies to share workstations instead of giving one desk to every employee.

But some employers are now moving in the other direction. They are bringing back assigned desks or using hot-desking less often.

This change has been reported at some companies. It was also discussed at an office conference, with comments from office and real estate leaders.

For employees, the complaint can be simple.

An open desk may change every day. Workers may sit beside people they do not know. One survey says employees can value a workspace that is predictable and consistent. They may also see hot-desking as less attractive than working from home.

These points help explain employee dissatisfaction. But they do not prove that one single factor caused it.

Hot-desking is still important in many workplaces. One report, citing workplace data, said the share of workers using hot-desking had doubled from before the pandemic, reaching 20%.

At the same time, this is not a full return to the old office.

The move back to assigned desks is limited to some companies and departments. Many businesses are still using shared desks and flexible space.

So the office story is now split.

Some teams want flexibility. Others want a clear place to sit.

### A desk can feel like more than furniture

One report found a link between assigned seating and two feelings: belonging and focus. Among workers with assigned desks, 87% reported a sense of belonging, compared with 74% in unassigned settings. The focus figures were 80% and 67%. The data shows a link, not proof of cause.

### The wider office is still sharing

A 2024 survey points in the other direction. The share of companies with one desk per employee or fewer fell from 56% in 2023 to 40% in 2024. Respondents expected it to reach about one-third by 2026. Desk sharing remains the wider pattern.

## In one line…

Hot-desking is not disappearing, but in some offices, the personal desk is quietly finding its way back into the plan.

# Young Travelers Want Trips at Their Own Pace — But Stays Are Still Short

A trip can feel slower before it becomes longer.

That is the tension in Japan’s youth travel picture as of September 2026. Young people, especially young men, increasingly want to travel at their own pace. But the available numbers on actual stays do not yet show a clear move to longer trips.

For these travelers, a good trip is not always about seeing as many famous places as possible. It can mean having room in the day and choosing what matters to them. Several surveys point to the same wish: more control and less pressure in the schedule.

But a wish is not the same as a travel pattern. Signs of a slower style are easier to see in what people say they want than in how long trips currently last. So this is not a finished change from sightseeing to slow travel. It is a gap between a new preference and current travel habits.

The pattern is not the same for all young people. Among women aged 29 and under, visiting famous tourist places remains popular, at about 45%. The strongest signal is among young men, while the overall picture is mixed.

### Slow travel can be about control

Here, “slow” does not always mean a long holiday. Among men aged 29 and under, about one in four chose solo travel, and a similar share chose a hobby-focused trip. Another survey found that about 90% of people aged 19 to 25 wanted free time in an overseas tour; most wanted half a day or more. This suggests that open time may matter as much as trip length.

### The real test is what people do

The key test is actual travel time, not an ideal answer. If people had a full month off, the most popular choice was about one week of travel, at about 24%. But people planning an autumn trip expected 1.8 nights on average, with a middle answer of 2 nights. The Tourism White Paper still lists longer stays as a policy need. The wish is clear, but it has not yet become a broad change in travel behavior.

## In one line

The clearest movement is toward more personal travel, especially among young men; the evidence for longer stays is still an emerging signal, not a completed shift.

# Young Japan Wants Slower Trips. The Plans Are Still Short

As of September 2026, a quiet split appears in travel surveys in Japan.

Young people are showing more interest in trips at their own pace. They want room for personal interests and free time. But the trips they plan are still often short.

This is the interesting part: wanting slower travel does not yet mean a long stay.

When people imagined getting a full month off, the most common answer was a trip of about one week. It was chosen by 24.1%. This shows that many people can imagine giving travel more time when the chance exists.

But a different autumn survey looked at people who were planning a trip. Their planned hotel stays averaged 1.8 nights, with a median of 2 nights.

The two pictures do not fully match. One shows a wish for more time. The other shows short plans.

Japan’s Tourism White Paper also says that making stays longer is still a policy task. So the evidence does not show a complete move from famous sightseeing to slow travel.

It shows a growing wish for a more personal trip, while long stays have not yet become normal.

### Slow can mean more control

Slow travel may be less about adding nights and more about choosing how to use the day. Among men aged 29 and under, solo travel was about 25%, and hobby-focused travel was about 24%. A separate survey found that about 90% of Gen Z respondents wanted free time inside an overseas tour. About 80% wanted at least half a day. A short trip can still feel more personal when the traveler has room to choose.

### One age group, different travel missions

Young travelers are not one single market. Women aged 29 and under still showed strong interest in famous tourist places, at about 45%. Gourmet travel was even higher, at about 52%. This is not the same picture as the male interest in solo and hobby-based trips. The useful lesson is not that sightseeing is ending. Different young travelers may be looking for different kinds of value from the same holiday.

## In one line…

The direction is visible in several surveys, but it is still a change in what young travelers want—not proof that long, slow stays have become the new normal.

# Young Japanese Travelers Want More Freedom, But Their Trips Are Still Short

As of September 2026, travel surveys in Japan tell a story with two different speeds.

Many younger travelers, especially men, seem to want more room for their own pace and interests. But the trips measured in surveys are still short.

This contrast appears clearly when people imagine having more time. In one survey, the most common answer was about one week of travel if people could take a one-month vacation. About 24% chose that answer.

But an autumn survey by the same research center asked about people considering a trip. Their planned stays averaged about 1.8 nights, with a median of about two nights.

These were not the same question. One measured a wish under a special condition. The other measured a current travel plan. Together, they show a gap between the trip people imagine and the time they plan to spend.

Japan’s Tourism White Paper also says the country needs more trips per person and longer stays. In other words, longer travel is still a policy goal, not a completed change in behavior.

So this is not a simple story about famous sightseeing being replaced by slow travel. The clearer story is that attitudes are changing faster than travel schedules.

### Slow travel is also about control

Slow travel here may mean control over time, not simply more nights. Men aged 29 and under put solo travel at 25.2%, while hobby-focused travel showed a similar pattern. Separately, about 90% of Gen Z respondents wanted free time during an overseas tour, and about 80% wanted half a day or more. A short package does not have to be fully scheduled.

### One youth market does not fit all

“Young Japanese travelers” is too broad a label. For men aged 18 to 29, solo travel was the leading travel arrangement in another survey. But among women aged 29 and under, 44.7% were still interested in visiting famous tourist spots. Different groups may respond to different offers: flexible, interest-led plans for some, and landmark-focused trips for others.

## In one line…

Young travelers in Japan are showing a clearer wish for more self-directed travel, especially young men, but the evidence points to an emerging preference—not a completed shift to longer stays.

# One Office, Two Ideas of a Place to Work

## The Question

Each morning, one worker enters the office and looks for an empty desk. Another chooses a quiet corner or a busy place near other teams. Some companies are bringing back personal desks. Others still use shared desks. Why does the same office feel safe to one person and free to another?

### One Voice: A desk that helps me start

Every morning, I look for an empty desk. Someone may have used it yesterday, and someone else may use it tomorrow. I cannot keep papers in a drawer. I sometimes worry about using a desk or keyboard after someone else. I spend time finding a place before work starts. I miss having the same desk, drawer, and view. They helped me start without looking around and gave me a quiet feeling that I belonged there. Now the office can feel like a place I only borrow. I want my work and things to have a place, even when I cannot choose the desk rules.

### Another Voice: Freedom to move

Some mornings, I choose a quiet corner because I need to think. On other days, I sit where talking is easy. A different desk can put me near people from another department. It can also give me space when a work relationship feels uncomfortable. Sometimes I simply need room. Working from home gave me a place of my own, so I do not need one fixed place at the office. I like changing my surroundings. I choose a place that fits my mood and task. I also choose who is near me—or whether I want anyone near me.

## Where the Difference Comes From

The disagreement is not really about moving. It is about the source of stability. One worker finds stability in a desk that stays in one place. Papers and a familiar start help this person. The other finds stability in the power to change who is nearby. The kind of space this person needs can also change each day. A shared-desk system can even lead people to use the same desk often. So a rule may look flexible on paper but feel difficult to one person. The same system may feel useful to another.

## What the Seat Really Means

The real question is not fixed desks or shared desks. It is what makes a place work. One person needs a steady point. It removes the need to search every day. Another needs enough control to change the people nearby and the work space. The seat is only the visible part of a deeper question: What makes a worker feel, “This is my place at work”?

Lena placed the small silver memory capsule on the kitchen table. Its surface was smooth and cold, with one blue line glowing around the lid.

Inside was the memory she could no longer carry: rain sliding down a hospital window, white lights above her, and her brother’s hand becoming still inside hers.

She had watched that moment too many times. Each time, the pain came back with the same force. So she connected the capsule to the memory-storage unit and waited.

A calm voice came from the unit. “Return date?” asked the storage robot.

Lena looked at the empty chair across from her. Her brother should have been sitting there, making some small joke about the weather.

“Five years from today,” she said.

The blue line stopped moving.

“Are you sure?” asked the storage robot.

Lena closed her eyes. “No,” she said. “But I cannot carry it now.”

The capsule grew warm in her hands. A soft light passed over it, and the memory disappeared into secure storage. The system locked it away until the date she had chosen.

At first, Lena felt guilty for being relieved. Then she began to feel free.

She returned to work. She made dinner without stopping in the middle of the room. At night, she slept for several hours at a time. Her brother still appeared in her dreams, but he was always far away. His face moved like a picture under deep water. Lena could see him, but she could not reach him.

Sometimes, she touched the capsule and wondered what it knew about her that she no longer knew about herself.

Then, five years later, on a cold morning, the capsule opened.

Lena was making tea when rain began to sound inside the kitchen.

The hospital returned—the hard lights, the sharp smell, the weight of her brother’s fingers in her hand. Then she heard his voice.

“Do not make my last day your whole life,” her brother said.

Lena dropped to the floor.

She had forgotten those words. For five years, she had remembered only the final breath and the empty bed. But the memory had kept more than the worst moment.

It continued. Her own younger voice spoke beside the hospital bed.

“I will come back to this,” her younger self said. “When I am ready, I will remember all of it.”

The storage robot offered a new return date.

Lena’s hand shook above the control. She could delay the memory again. But would that be healing, or would she only leave the frightened woman she had been alone in the dark?

She did not press the button.

On the kitchen floor, she listened to the rain, to her brother’s last words, and to her younger voice. That earlier Lena had not been healed, but she had known the way back.

For the first time, Lena let the pain stay with the love.

# Why Silence Can Feel Uncomfortable

A conversation can be going well. Then someone finishes a sentence, and no one answers.

In one 2011 experiment, 102 undergraduate students imagined a group conversation. After a mildly controversial comment, some students read that the conversation continued normally. Others read that a brief silence followed. The silence group reported more feelings of rejection and negative emotion. They also reported less belonging, lower self-esteem, and less agreement with the group.

A second experiment showed a similar pattern in a more realistic setting. Thirty-seven students watched a six-minute conversation. In one version, a single silence lasted four seconds. Afterward, those students reported more rejection and negative emotion, and less positive emotion and belonging. Most were not aware of the exact pause.

But a long pause does not always feel bad. A 2023 study looked at natural ten-minute conversations between strangers and friends. Gaps of more than two seconds were more common among friends. For strangers, these longer gaps reduced the feeling of connection. For friends, they increased it. People who watched the conversations also judged long pauses between strangers as more awkward.

The same question appears when people are alone. Across 11 studies, participants generally did not enjoy spending six to fifteen minutes with nothing to do but think. They often rated simple activities as more enjoyable. In one study, 55 students sat alone for 15 minutes with the option of giving themselves a mild electric shock they had already experienced. Many chose the shock instead of remaining without outside stimulation. That was a result from this experiment, not a claim about everyone.

At the same time, silence can also bring calm. In one study of roughly 46 students, six minutes and 30 seconds of silence increased relaxation in both a university room and a city garden. The outdoor setting also brought less boredom and a stronger feeling of being in the present moment.

Research on the body shows the same mixed picture. A review of 37 studies found that responses to silence depend on the kind of silence, the setting, familiarity, surrounding noise, and other personal factors. In a study that measured heart activity, one noise condition showed more activity linked with the body’s calming system than silence, while white noise showed more activity linked with its alerting system than that noise.

People also differ across studies and cultures. In a study of 2,557 college students at 12 sites in 11 countries, an everyday activity was enjoyed more than thinking for pleasure in every country tested. Still, differences between countries were linked with personal factors such as openness, meditation experience, starting mood, and phone use. In one Japan–United States survey, views of silence also changed depending on whether people were speaking with strangers or close friends.

### When Quiet Has Structure

The key distinction is not silence itself, but whether it is chosen and mentally structured. Across four studies, actively choosing solitude was associated with relaxation and lower stress. In another study, students told to occupy their thoughts for a brief period reported better mood, greater relaxation, and lower arousal afterward. Quiet can therefore function differently when people have agency and a mental path to follow.

### Context Over Country

A staged one-to-one tutorial complicates any simple cultural story. Japanese and UK undergraduates differed by only about seven seconds in their mean tolerance of an instructor’s silence. Both groups reported similar discomfort, around 4 on a six-point scale, and longer silence was not linked to greater discomfort. Nationality alone, then, is a weak guide when roles and setting change.

## In one line

Silence is not a universal signal; before judging the pause, listen for the situation that gives it meaning.

# If You Had to Watch a Stone for Five Minutes, Would Your “Bad-Guy Switch” Turn On?

A stone. Still a stone. Surely something will happen soon—but no, it’s a stone. Nothing happens on the screen. This goes on for five minutes. But you, the viewer, can still do one thing: make someone else’s reward smaller.

This suddenly sounds dark. But it comes from an online experiment with people in the United States. They were put into groups at random. One group watched a five-minute video of a stone, where nothing happened. The other group watched a magician.

During the video, they had three choices. They could make another person’s reward smaller, make it bigger, or do nothing. They could change it by 10 cents each time, up to 50 cents in all. The stone on the screen stayed quiet, while the viewers were given “a little power.”

So, did boredom become fuel for being mean?

People who strongly liked seeing others suffer were more likely to make the other person’s reward smaller after watching the stone video than after watching the magician video. For people who felt this less strongly, there was no clear difference.

You may want to say, “So, it really depends on personality.” But there is more to the story.

In the next experiment, people were again put into groups at random. But this time, they could not make the reward bigger. They could only make it smaller. This time, it did not matter how strongly people liked seeing others suffer. People who watched the stone video were more likely to make another person’s reward smaller than people in the other groups.

If we look only at personality, we may miss something. We need to ask not only what kind of person someone is, but also what they can do in that situation. We thought we were reading a profile of the person. Now we also notice how the stage is set.

But it is too soon to say, “Add a button to make rewards bigger and bring world peace!” The two were separate experiments. We cannot say the choices alone caused the different results. We do not know if giving people a choice to make rewards bigger can stop meanness.

The experiment looked only at brief boredom. It also looked only at actions that made another person’s reward smaller. We cannot use its results directly to explain everyday meanness or boredom that lasts a long time.

Even so, we see boring moments a little differently now. We can ask not only, “What mustn’t I do?” but also, “What else can I do instead?” Before we look at someone’s personality, we can look at the menu in front of us. The stone may not move for five minutes. But the question we ask changes a little.

## In one line
Stone-watchers were more likely to make another person’s reward smaller. In one test, this was true only for people who strongly liked seeing others suffer; in another, it was true at every level. The tests suggest choices may matter along with personality, but they do not show that offering a choice to make rewards bigger stops meanness or applies to everyday life.

# The Coffee Price Rise Case: Turn Back the Clock on the Price Tag!

You go to buy your usual coffee, but then you stop. “Hey, when did you become so fancy?” Tariffs are the first thing you think of. You want to say, “So, you’re to blame!” But a good detective stops and thinks first. Let’s turn back the clock and examine this case.

Reports based on government figures say the average U.S. price of ground coffee rose 41%. That was compared with the same month a year earlier. This is about ground coffee, not a cup in a café. Before coffee wakes you up, its price shocks your wallet awake.

But Reuters says most of the rise in store prices came from bean shortages and higher bean prices. Those shortages began before the summer tariffs. Wait a minute. Our case began before the suspect we watched even appeared.

The investigation leads us to Brazil. A drought was happening there. People had also stopped hoping that the next harvest would be better. “Will there be enough beans?” Before we think about how to brew them, we must ask if there will be any beans to brew at all.

We turn the pages of the record and find this. In February, before summer, New York’s Arabica coffee futures price reached a record high. This was not the price of ground coffee in stores. It was the market price for trading coffee beans. The market alarm had already sounded.

“So, were tariffs not to blame?” No. That would be deciding too soon, too. Reuters also reported that U.S. tariffs put in place during summer raised the price of the beans themselves. They did play a part. But we must put events in the right order.

Here is the key point. At the time of that report, the tariff-caused rise had not yet passed through the whole supply chain. It had not fully reached the prices shoppers paid. When bean costs rise, the store price tag does not jump up at once and say, “Got it!” Price rises take time to appear.

In other words, a price tag is not live news. It is like a letter that arrives a little late. You may open it today, but it may not be about something that happened today. It may tell you about an earlier drought, a bean shortage, or high market prices. If you look only at the latest headline, you may name the wrong sender.

Next time, take a second look at a store price tag. Ask, “Why is it expensive?” Then add, “When did this happen?” Coffee may taste bitter, but we want our detective work to be clear. Before that first cup, turn the clock back a little.

## In one line
The average U.S. price of ground coffee rose 41% from a year earlier, mostly because beans were scarce and cost more. Tariffs also raised bean prices, but their full effect had not reached shoppers, so tags may show older events.

# Coffee Bean Prices Fall. Are Price Tags Still on a Journey?

“Beans have gotten cheaper!” At that news, your wallet pumps its fist. In your mind, the price of your usual cup has already come down, too. But the price tag in a shop may not change right away. When you see a price tag that makes you want to say, “Haven’t you heard the news?”, it seems there is a time lag.

The price measure reported by the International Coffee Organization fell 8.7% from the previous month. The reason, it said, was that more beans harvested in Brazil had entered the market, and a good supply was expected to continue.

The US Department of Agriculture said that earlier high prices came from several factors happening at once: bad weather in Brazil and Vietnam, fewer beans available for sale, and strong demand.

Meanwhile, US consumer price data showed that the price of coffee was 6.1% higher than in the same month a year earlier. It may leave you wondering, “Did prices go down or up?” But the data covers a different month from the bean price measure. And it does not show the price of a cup at a cafe. Hold on before putting the two figures in the ring.

So, how long does it take for the price of beans to reach a price tag?

According to estimates from market insiders and experts interviewed by Reuters, it takes at least about nine months for the price of raw beans to show up in US retail prices. The road to a price tag is quite a long journey.

The article says that companies in the US that roast coffee keep raw beans in stock. Roasting and packing the beans also take time. They also often negotiate prices with retailers on a regular basis. The price tag in a shop does not flash to a new price the moment the market moves.

However, the “about nine months” figure is an estimate based on interviews. It is not a rule that applies to every company, and it is not a promise that “prices will fall in nine months.” It is too soon to mark the date on your calendar.

And a cup at a cafe comes with costs besides the beans. One cafe operator in Chicago said that the cost of cups and labor, as well as the cost of buying beans, had been behind price increases. Even if bean prices fall, other costs do not always fall along with them.

If you are waiting for the price of your usual cup to come down, think not only, “How much do beans cost now?” but also, “When does the price of the beans reach here?” A coffee price tag may have an unseen clock of its own, separate from the latest news about the market.

## In one line
Falling coffee bean prices may take at least nine months to affect US retail prices.

# If You Didn’t Write with AI, You Can’t Apply

What if the rules for entering a literary prize included a condition like this? Not “You may use AI,” but “Write together with AI.” Wait, that’s required? AI, which I thought was a helper behind the scenes, is now openly the ticket to enter.

The Prix Pascal, whose creation was announced in France, is for unpublished fiction in French written jointly by a human and AI. Using AI is not a bonus or an exception. If you haven’t used it, you can’t apply.

It may be too early to brace yourself for “At last, it’s time to compete over AI’s writing skills.” What I’m curious about is not the writers, but the people giving the prize. Why did they go out of their way to create this kind of entrance?

The people behind the prize say it is an effort to ask other literary prizes, which are struggling with how to handle writers’ use of AI, a question. They create one prize and ask the others, “So, what would you do?” You might call it a question in the shape of a trophy.

For example, what if you were reading a story late into the night, and just after the last line moved you, you heard, “Actually, I wrote it with AI”? Would a line that had seemed beautiful suddenly feel distant? Or would you say, “I enjoyed it, so I have no complaint”? A special judging meeting might begin inside the reader’s mind.

Of course, the label “co-written with AI” alone doesn’t guarantee an interesting story. I wouldn’t decide I wanted to read it based on that alone, either. What I want to know is what kind of story it is, and what the writing is like. Before the label, I want to see the first page.

But when I take the writer’s side, things suddenly get complicated. I might ask AI to fix a phrase or talk through the plot. But how far can I go and still proudly say, “I wrote this”? Where is the line between a helpful partner to talk things over with and a co-writer?

So it would be a shame to reduce this prize to a simple choice: “Is AI good or bad?” A prize that is supposed to choose works also shines a light on the values of the people doing the choosing. It makes the question of whether AI was used not the end of the discussion, but the starting point for reading. It seems that writers are not the only ones being tested at this new entrance. So, how will we read that book?

## In one line
France has announced a literary prize requiring unpublished French fiction to be co-written by a person and AI. Its founders say it challenges other awards over AI, while inviting readers to consider how AI changes the way they read.

# Could Musk’s “Good Idea” Jam Up Merger Talks?

“If the boss is eager, things move fast.” It’s a familiar hope in meetings and business talks. But in talks about bringing Tesla and SpaceX together, that hope may be turned on its head. You think you’ve stepped on the gas, but the brake lights come on. Concerns are emerging about that kind of turn of events.

Musk supported combining the two companies, calling it “a good idea.” However, he says the decision should be left to the special committees of the two companies. Don’t jump to conclusions. There are still hurdles to clear between “he supports it” and “the merger is decided.”

According to Reuters, a person familiar with the talks is concerned that Musk’s statement of support and the public announcement of the talks could make shareholders look more closely, slowing the negotiations. Support from a big name does not always mean things will suddenly move ahead. Note that this is not a report that talks have already been delayed.

The louder the support, the more attention it draws. When the star of the show steps into the spotlight, people in the audience watch more closely. Will people think, “If Musk supports it, we can relax,” or “Wait, let’s check the details”? What matters is not how loud the support is, but the response it gets.

To begin with, the special committees of both companies are there to consider the merger. Setting them up does not mean the merger has been approved. To put it another way, they have only reached the stage of setting out chairs for a review meeting. It’s too early to pop the party poppers.

Shareholder approval also has to follow certain steps. For example, for certain mergers and other matters, SpaceX’s articles of incorporation require approval from holders of “Class B” shares voting as a separate group, as well as any other required approvals. Musk’s support is not a pass that opens every gate.

We do not know whether talks will really be delayed this time. So what to watch next is not just “Is Musk in favor?” but “How will others act in response to that support?” Will the cheering voices build momentum, or will closer checks lead to cautious driving? A big name’s words can fire the starting gun, or give people a reason to stop. Precisely because someone has spoken in favor, we can’t take our eyes off the reactions that follow in these merger talks.

## In one line
Musk called a Tesla-SpaceX merger “a good idea,” but the deal is still under review. A person familiar with the talks worries that his support and the public announcement could draw closer shareholder scrutiny and slow negotiations, though no delay has been reported.

# Is Your Video Putting on an Unwanted Show on the Train?

You get on the train and find a seat. At last, you can relax—or so you think. Then you hear sounds from a video somewhere: laughter, sound effects, and cheerful music in the background. You are quietly going home. But your ears have to log in to someone else’s video suggestions. You paid for a train ticket, but you don’t remember paying to see this show.

One smartphone makes the whole train carriage an audience. That’s a pretty bold show.

Here’s news about this kind of “sound no one asked for.” On October 19, 2026, the UK announced the start of a national campaign. It asks train passengers to use headphones.

But don’t quickly think, “In the UK, no headphones means you’re breaking the law!” No new rule bans all sound. The campaign points to current rail rules and asks people to think about others.

Current rail rules ban sounds from a device when they bother other people. They may cover sound from a phone speaker, too, if the situation fits the rules. There is an exception when the train company has given written permission. A song may sound like a masterpiece to you, but not to the person beside you.

If you break the rules, you could get a fine of up to £1,000. That’s enough to make you reach for your wallet before the volume button. But remember the words “up to” and “could.” It doesn’t mean everyone who plays sound on a speaker gets a £1,000 fine.

So the first step is a call to use headphones. People will see the message on posters and hear it in announcements at stations and on trains. The fine may be what people hear most, but let’s hear the campaign’s message, too.

Its name means something like, “Share the journey, not the noise.” Just because we’re in the same carriage doesn’t mean we’ve joined the fan club for the same video. The words draw that line simply.

This isn’t saying, “Don’t enjoy yourself.” It’s more like saying, “Choose who hears the sound.” You can enjoy videos and music. Just don’t make people around you sit in the audience without asking them. Headphones don’t take away your entertainment. They’re a small screen that keeps the fun in your own seat.

The next time you press play, take a breath. “Who am I sending this sound to?” We’re on the same train, going the same way. Still, the sound doesn’t have to ride into everyone else’s ears.

## In one line
The UK has started a national campaign asking train passengers to use headphones, not banning all sound. It asks people to enjoy videos and music without making other passengers listen.

In a small kingdom, the ruler, Dionysius, was afraid of enemies. If anyone spoke against him, his guards could take that person to prison. Often, the ruler ordered executions without a fair trial.

One day, a shepherd named Melos stood before him.

“You punish people before you know the truth,” Melos said. “That is not justice.”

The ruler’s face became hard. “Then you will die.”

Melos’s sister was going to be married in three days. He fell to his knees.

“Please let me go to her wedding,” he said. “I will return before my death.”

The ruler laughed. “Why should I believe you?”

Melos’s friend, Selinuntius, stepped forward. “I will stay here in his place.”

So the ruler agreed. Melos had three days to go and return. If he did not come back, his friend would die.

Melos ran from the city. He reached the river, but heavy rain had made the water wild. The small boat broke against a rock. Melos fell into the cold river and nearly disappeared under the water. At last, he reached the other side, shaking and weak.

He hurried to the wedding. He smiled for his sister, but his eyes stayed on the road. When the wedding ended, he left at once.

On the way back, three attackers jumped from behind some trees. They took his horse and pushed him to the ground. Melos tried to stand, but pain filled his body. He walked through the night, then fell beside the road.

The sky was becoming bright. The time was almost finished.

Melos looked toward the city. “I cannot do this,” he whispered. “Perhaps my friend is already dead.”

For a moment, he wanted to hide in the forest.

Then he remembered his friend’s calm face. His friend had trusted him enough to face death.

“No,” Melos said. “I gave my word.”

He stood and ran.

At the city gate, the guards were leading his friend to the place of execution. Then Melos shouted, “Wait!”

Everyone turned. Melos fell before the ruler.

“I promised to return,” he said. “I am here.”

The ruler looked at the two friends. Slowly, he lowered his hand.

“Free him,” he said.

After that day, the ruler demanded fair trials. He had learned that trust and loyalty could be stronger than fear.

Melos called across the hall, “You kill men from fear. You never give them a chance to speak.”

Silence came, and guards grabbed the young shepherd. The ruler ordered his death.

“Give me three days to see my sister’s wedding,” Melos said. “Then I will return to you.”

The ruler smiled and said, “Your friend must stay here. Return late, and he will die in your place.”

Melos turned to his friend, who offered his hands for the chains. Melos had no time to speak.

“Go now, because I know you will come back.”

At the wedding, his sister’s laugh rose above everyone’s voices. Melos listened closely to remember its exact sound.

He left for the city before daylight on day three.

The river stopped him; its bridge was gone. Rain made the water brown and dangerously fast. He stepped back, ran, and jumped into the flood.

The water pulled him under, but he fought toward the light. He grabbed a branch and pulled himself onto the far bank.

Later, three men blocked his way, and a knife flashed. He hit the man holding it with his walking stick. He ran uphill as their shouts followed behind him.

By afternoon, each step hurt, and his feet were bloody. He fell beside a rock and tried to stand. But his legs would not lift him.

He could wait here, and someone might find him. Or he could return home.

But his friend would lose his life instead.

For one awful moment, that felt easier than standing up.

He remembered the hands held out for the chains. His friend trusted him without asking for another promise.

Water came slowly through a crack in the rock. Melos drank, got onto his knees, and stood up.

He managed one step, then took another.

At the city gates, the bell rang for his friend’s death.

He raced to the square, where the sword was already raised above his friend.

“Stop now! I’m back!”

His friend turned around, and Melos fell against him.

“I almost left you to die,” he said softly.

“I almost lost my trust in you,” his friend replied.

They held each other while the last sun lit the walls.

The ruler kept his eyes on them.

Finally, he said, “Put the sword down and free both men.”

More softly, he then asked, “How can a man win such trust?”

For once, he waited for a reply instead of demanding one.

So the ruler agreed. Melos had three days to go and return. If he did not come back, his friend would die.

Melos ran from the city. He reached the river, but heavy rain had made the water wild. The small boat broke against a rock. Melos fell into the cold river and nearly disappeared under the water. At last, he reached the other side, shaking and weak.

He hurried to the wedding. He smiled for his sister, but his eyes stayed on the road. When the wedding ended, he left at once.

On the way back, three attackers jumped from behind some trees. They took his horse and pushed him to the ground. Melos tried to stand, but pain filled his body. He walked through the night, then fell beside the road.

The sky was becoming bright. The time was almost finished.

Melos looked toward the city. “I cannot do this,” he whispered. “Perhaps my friend is already dead.”

For a moment, he wanted to hide in the forest.

Then he remembered his friend’s calm face. His friend had trusted him enough to face death.

“No,” Melos said. “I gave my word.”

He stood and ran.

At the city gate, the guards were leading his friend to the place of execution. Then Melos shouted, “Wait!”

Everyone turned. Melos fell before the ruler.

“I promised to return,” he said. “I am here.”

The ruler looked at the two friends. Slowly, he lowered his hand.

“Free him,” he said.

After that day, the ruler demanded fair trials. He had learned that trust and loyalty could be stronger than fear.

### The Lemon on the Books

I had a little money, a bad cough, and a heavy feeling in my chest. I walked through Kyoto without knowing where to go. The streets were wet from the morning rain. Every few minutes, I stopped to catch my breath.

I liked old things. A faded red sign, a blue cup in a shop window, a worn green coat—these things seemed more alive than new ones. They made me feel less alone.

On Teramachi Street, I found a small fruit shop. Bright oranges and apples stood in wooden boxes. Near the door, a basket held lemons. They were a deep, shining yellow.

I went inside and asked the shopkeeper for one lemon. It cost more than I wanted to pay, but I bought it.

The lemon was cool in my hand. Its fresh smell rose up to my face. For a few moments, I felt awake. I turned it over and watched the yellow skin catch the light.

Then I walked to Maruzen, the big bookshop. I had been there many times. Inside, the rows of books seemed to close around me. I saw familiar covers and remembered bills I could not pay. My chest felt heavy again.

I thought I should leave. But I did not move.

Instead, I began to pile books on a table. One, then another, then another. The pile grew tall and leaned a little to one side. My hands shook as I placed one more book on top.

I looked at the lemon in my hand.

What if I put it on the tower?

Carefully, I set it on the highest book. It sat there, bright and round. For a second, I could not breathe. The lemon seemed to be a tiny bomb. In my mind, it would burst—not with fire, but with a yellow flash. Every book in Maruzen would rise into the air, and all my worries would fly away with them.

Nothing happened.

The books stayed still. The lemon did not move.

I stepped back, then turned and walked out. I left the lemon on the tower.

On the street, I began to laugh. My cough still hurt, and I was still short of money. But the weight in my chest had grown lighter. Behind me, the little yellow bomb waited quietly among the books.

# “Can’t Wait for the Next Episode”? Make One Yourself? “byUs” Lets You Shape Stories with Characters You Love

“Wait, it ends here!?” Have you ever blurted that out when a manga ends at an exciting moment and says the story will continue next time? What will that character say next? What will happen to the two of them? It might be a shame to let those ideas stay only in your head.

The company that runs LINE Manga has announced the launch of “byUs,” an AI story chat service. It is pronounced “bias.” You can enjoy talking with your favorite characters and make your own stories based on the works. You can take a step from the reader’s seat onto the stage of story-making.

If you thought, “Can’t you already talk with characters?” you’ve noticed something important. LINE Manga already has “Character Chat.” The company says the difference is that, as well as having conversations, you can make stories more freely. In other words, you can enjoy not only asking, “What should we talk about next?” but also, “What should happen next?”

For example, you can continue an official story in the service. Or you can make your own story as a fan. “What if that person showed up here?” “If it were me, I’d want to see this happen.” The ideas that grew with every turn of the page can now become a starting point for your own stories. The time spent waiting for what happens next may become time spent thinking up what happens next.

What’s more, you can publish the fan stories you make if you want to. You can enjoy them privately, or let someone else read them. But things change when you make a story public. “Will people understand this plot?” “I want to work on what happens next a little more.” You may find yourself thinking like a story-maker before you know it, even though you started out as a reader.

Of course, you can’t bring in just anything you like. Only works and characters approved by their original creators can be used. The Help page also explains that the service has permission to use the original works it features through formal agreements with their creators. This is the foundation that lets you enjoy freely imagining “what if.”

The service first offered two works and four characters in Japan. “Taking part in a story” here means moving the story forward through conversation or making a story as a fan. The fun of reading a work is joined by the fun of thinking up what happens next.

Until now, “If it were me, I’d do it this way” was something you could only say to yourself. With byUs, those words become a way into making a story. What will you say to a character you love? What will happen next in the story? So, where will your “next part” begin?

## In one line
LINE Manga has launched byUs, an AI service that lets readers chat with approved characters and create stories based on their works. It gives readers a way to imagine what happens next and make fan stories they can keep private or share.

# A Human Joined an AI Phone Call. The Problem Was the “Cast Change” Notice

I was impressed: “AI can even make phone calls. The future is here!” But the person handling the request on the other end of the line was human. Wait—what a sudden change of genre, from science fiction to a workplace drama. Still, the heart of this story is not “So it was a human after all!” It is whether people were properly told about the change in who was taking part.

Meta was testing some calls made through Muse in which trained contract workers made the calls and completed the conversations with the other person. They tested a setup where Muse handed the work over to a human agent. Not all calls were handled by humans. It’s too soon to put up a caption saying, “Actually, it was all done by people!”

But one important notice was missing from this test. The vice president of Meta’s Superintelligence Labs division admitted in an internal post that starting a test in which contract workers made calls without proper disclosure was a “mistake.” The vice president also said that Meta had rolled back its human concierge feature for now.

Let’s check the breaking-news caption once more. What they pulled back was the human concierge feature. They did not stop all calls through Muse. Canceling an entire show and pausing one segment are two different things.

So, is it bad in itself to bring in a human helper? There may be times when handing things to a person helps move the conversation forward. But there is a big difference between telling someone, “A person will take over from here,” and quietly changing the cast backstage. In a movie, you might clap and say, “Ah, so that’s who it is!” when a mysterious person is revealed. But you may not want a surprise reveal in a conversation you are part of.

Some people may choose their words or feel differently when they think they are talking to AI than when they know they are talking to a person. Even if the request is handled without a problem, that does not mean the disclosure issue can be brushed aside with “it all worked out in the end.” That was exactly the point Meta itself admitted it had got wrong.

Convenience matters. But for some people, knowing who they are talking to matters just as much. If AI hands the baton to a person, that one line saying so is part of the service, too. The person taking over does not have to be a secret guest.

## In one line
Meta admitted it was a mistake to have contractors handle some Muse calls without telling the people they called.

# Phones Handed In in the Morning: Different Voices

I want my daughter's high school to hold onto the phones. Collect them all in the morning. Give them back when school lets out. Until then, they stay handed in. Then I wouldn't be the only bad guy. We agreed that at night, she'd put her phone in a basket in the living room. My daughter didn't keep that promise. I took her phone away. The next morning, breakfast was quiet. All I could hear was the sound of dishes. I wanted her to stick to what we'd agreed, but after I took her phone, I was the one who couldn't look her in the face. I don't want another morning like that. It would help if I could say the school was doing the same thing. I'm tired of arguing every night. But I just want to push this onto the school. At work, I'm the one who makes the arrangements. At home, I want to get out of being the bad guy. I'm a dad asking the school to come to my rescue.

“I'm sleepy,” they say. Every morning, I see the faces of kids who come to the nurse's office first thing, and I wonder what else is behind that word. The other day, a phone screen was glowing beside the pillow of a child resting on a bed. I couldn't look away from that glow. I wanted to ask about last night, but what would happen if they thought I was a teacher who takes phones away? Would they still talk to me? If we collect all the phones in the morning and don't give them back until school lets out, can we say that's enough? I'm afraid that once we've collected the phones, we'll think everything is fine. I want that child to be able to talk about what happens at night. I don't want the nurse's office to be a place where phones are taken away. After we take a phone in, who will listen to that child?

I sort packages in a warehouse during the day, and go to evening high school at night. But I can't hand in my phone until school lets out. I can keep my promise not to touch it during class. During breaks, I want to answer work messages. Before, calls from work kept coming during class. I couldn't answer, and the missed calls just kept piling up on my screen. Later, they told me it was a problem that they couldn't reach me. I almost had my shifts cut. I give the money I earn to my family. I want to earn my workplace's trust myself. But I don't want to quit school. I've started to understand the lessons here. I don't want to choose between work and school. I promise I'll keep my phone at the bottom of my bag during class. So please listen to what I have to say before deciding.

At the breakfast table, beside the pillow in the nurse's office, and when work messages come, people want to stay able to talk to the other person. The school's phone collection might reduce arguments over the basket at night, but it could cut off a conversation by the pillow. It might protect learning in class, but if it also stops messages about shifts during breaks, trust at work could be shaken. The father asking the school for help also doesn't want to go through the silence after taking the phone away again. They may disagree about how long phones should be handed in, but they share a wish to still have someone they can talk to. What message do you want to answer right away? When does it come, and who sends it?

## In one line
A father wants his daughter’s school to collect phones all day, while a nurse and a working student worry about what that could interrupt. They disagree about when phones should be handed in, but all want to stay able to talk to someone.
